HIdentification. Handling and Transportation of Samples
IDisposal of specimen
  • Introduction

A specimen is defined as: “Any bodily substance taken from a person for the purpose of analysis, such as blood or urine”.

Specimens can therefore pose a risk to all staff handling them, from Reception Staff to Laboratory Staff.

To minimize these risks, the Practice will ensure that staff who handle specimens will be appropriately trained.

  • Collection and Storage

Specimen Collection and Labeling Collection Procedure

Follow standard aseptic techniques for specimen collection.

Use the appropriate containers for different types of specimens:

Blood samples: Use sterile vacutainer tubes (EDTA, citrate, or plain) depending on the

test.

Urine samples: Use sterile urine cups.

Tissue samples: Place in formalin-filled jars or sterile containers.

Swabs: Place in sterile swab tubes with the appropriate transport medium (e.g., viral, bacterial, or fungal transport medium).

For accurate results to be obtained, specimens should be received by the laboratory within 24 hours maximum, as after this period, the environmental organisms (such as e.coli) will form and flourish, whilst the weaker organisms (e.g. anaerobes), will die off. Consequently a false result will be obtained.

  • Request Forms and Containers

Specimens sent to the laboratory often cause concern for laboratory staff by either being sent in the incorrect packaging, or by not including the correct information.

The patient / service users’ details must be placed on both the specimen container and the specimen request form.

The specimen must be placed in a plastic bag with the request form in the separate pouch which is attached.

Specimen containers should include the patient' name And or UHID Number.

  • The request for analysis form must include:
    • Patient name and UHID number;
    • Patient’s GP and requesting Practitioner;
    • The location, to enable correct reporting of results;
    • Relevant clinical details, including planned or previous antibiotic therapy, date of onset of symptoms and specimen type;
    • Date and time the specimen was taken.

Failure to provide this information may result in specimens not being processed, delay specimen processing or lead to inappropriate tests being performed.

Specimens known or suspected to contain high risk pathogens, (e.g. blood borne viruses, tuberculosis, salmonella typhi), should be handled carefully.

  • Patient Information

Within the Practice environment patient need to be advised on appropriate specimen collection and should always be given the appropriate container.

Ideally, a designated specimen return area should be available, such as a plastic box that can be easily cleaned in case of spillage or contamination.

The patient should be encouraged to place the specimen in the container, or sample bag to reduce potential staff contact; leaking and broken specimens should be placed into the clinical waste system and any spillage cleaned up promptly.

Specimens must not be stored near food or drink.

Hand Alcohol Gel will be available for staff at all times and must be utilised after each sample collection taken, to avoid infection.

  • Blood

All samples of blood are to be in the approved sample tubes provided, which are sealed by a top. Should leakage of blood occur, due to imperfections in the bottle or incorrect fitting of the top, the sample must not be transported out of the Practice in the container.

All sample tubes containing blood are to be inserted into an approved bag, which is sealed to minimise the risk of contamination of personnel, should leakage occur.

If there is leakage or a spillage, subsequent action will depend on its extent.

If the leak is contained within the plastic bag, the bag is not to be opened and is to be inserted within another plastic bag, which is then sealed.

  • A suitable person (doctor / nurse) is to be informed when a leak occurs and will decide whether to dispose of the sample, or to transfer the remains of the sample into another bottle.
  • Such a transfer of blood must only be undertaken when the risk of contamination of personnel is minimal and when gloves are used; otherwise the sample is to be disposed of as above in a plastic bag and inserted into the sharps box.

If the leak is not contained within the bag and therefore contaminates either the outside of the bag or external objects, the following action is to be taken:

Avoid any further contamination by containing the sample within another plastic bag - if possible without undoing the bag. Tighten the top of the tube as this may be loose.

Dispose of the sample within an approved sharps box.

Ensure that hands are washed thoroughly with hot water and / or alcohol gel or soap. Any cut or open wound that comes into contact with the patient's blood must be thoroughly washed to ensure that none of the patient's blood remains in contact with the wound.

Any contaminated objects should be cleaned and disinfected.

All blood should be treated as high risk and universal precautions applied.

  • Urine

Although Urine, whether non-infected or infected, poses less of a risk than blood, sensible precautions should still be taken to avoid contamination of personnel or their clothing.

Gloves should be worn when handling urine containers as it is impossible to tell whether or not the container is contaminated with blood or faces.

  • Urine Samples in Sealed Containers

Samples of urine in sealed containers should pose no health risk, provided that the bottle is adequately sealed and no urine contaminates the outside of the bottle.

Pregnancy tests and dipstick testing make necessary the opening of urine bottles and exposure of personnel to urine. Gloves are always to be worn whilst testing urine and hands must always be washed after handling and testing urine.

  • Disposal of Urine

Urine is to be disposed of down the sluice or toilet. Under no circumstances may it to be disposed of down a sink.

  • Disposal of Urine Containers

Urine containers are disposable and are to be used once only. Urine bottles are to be emptied when analysis is complete and the bottle resealed and disposed of in the sharps bin.

  • Disposal of Dipsticks

Dipsticks should be disposed of in a clinical waste bag.

  • Faeces

Faeces pose a risk to medical personnel. Through faeces, a number of diseases are transmitted that can be serious (though they are rarely as serious as blood diseases). It is important to handle faeces specimens correctly to avoid the risk of disease.

  • Faeces Samples

Patients must provide their faeces sample(s) inside a specimen pot - No other container is acceptable.

Before defecation, the Patient / Service User should label their specimen container with their name, date of birth and date and time of production.

The specimen must then be placed inside a specimen pot and sealed by the Patient.

The Patient will be advised to wash their hands thoroughly after defecation, but before touching the specimen pot, and again after inserting the specimen pot into the bag.

  • Microbiological Swabs

Because swabs are taken of many infected areas of the body to assess the cause of the infection, a swab by definition therefore contains an unknown hazard.

Provided the swab is not removed from the transport medium, no risk of transmission of infection exists, unless there has been contamination of the outside of the container.

The following guidelines are to be implemented:

The top of the bottle must be sealed adequately before insertion into a sealed plastic hazard bag.

The form that accompanies the swab is to be placed in the appropriate pocket of the bag and not in the same compartment as the swab.

In the event of the top becoming loose and parting from the container whilst in the bag, the top is to be re-sealed either through the bag, or by opening the bag.

The transport medium is solid and unlikely to leak out of the bag. However, in the unlikely event of such an occurrence, it has to be assumed that microbiological material has also leaked. Therefore the specimen is to be disposed of and re-taken.

1. General Guidelines for All Specimens

  • All specimens must be treated as potentially infectious; follow universal precautions at all times.
  • Perform hand hygiene before and after specimen handling.
  • Use appropriate Personal Protective Equipment (PPE).

Labeling Requirements

All specimen containers must be clearly labeled with:

  • Patient Name
  • UHID (Unique Hospital Identification Number)
  • Date and Time of Sample Collection

Specimen Requisition Form

Every specimen must be accompanied by a duly completed request form including:

  • Patient details (Name, UHID)
  • Specimen type
  • Clinical information / provisional diagnosis
  • Date and time of collection
  • Relevant medication or therapy details

Packaging

  • Use appropriate containers based on specimen type.
  • Place specimen in a plastic biohazard bag.
  • Keep the request form in a separate pouch of the bag.

2. Outpatient Sample Collection

  • Verify patient identity and consent before collection.
  • Label the container prior to sample collection.
  • Use sterile equipment and maintain aseptic technique.
  • Collect specimen carefully to avoid contamination.
  • Place sample in an approved container and then into a plastic transport bag.
  • Ensure no leakage or contamination.
  • Send specimen to laboratory immediately, or store under recommended conditions if delay is unavoidable.

3. Inpatient Sample Collection

  • Samples must be collected by trained staff nurse or phlebotomist.
  • Follow standard aseptic techniques strictly.

Ensure the Sample Is:

  • Collected in the correct container
  • Properly sealed and labeled
  • Documented in:
    • Patient case file
    • Laboratory register/log

Transportation

  • Transport samples in a designated transport box with:
    • Biohazard labeling
    • Temperature control

Environmental Conditions During Transport

  • Maintain appropriate temperature conditions for different specimens:
  • Room temperature (15–25°C): Blood, swabs, and most routine samples.
  • Refrigerated (2–8°C): Urine, stool, and other samples requiring cold storage.
  • Frozen (-20°C or below): Plasma or serum for certain specialized tests (e.g., hormone analysis).
  • Use insulated coolers or temperature-controlled transport boxes for samples requiring cold storage or freezing.

4. Blood Sample Collection

  • Use vacutainers or sealed blood collection tubes only.
  • Ensure proper tube selection as per test requirement.

In Case of Leakage

  • Do not open the contaminated bag.
  • Place the sample into a second sealed biohazard bag.
  • Inform the doctor/nurse for decision on disposal or re-collection.

Safety Measures

  • Always wear gloves during collection and handling.
  • Treat all blood samples as high-risk (universal precautions).
  • Dispose of leaking or spilled samples in a sharps container.

5. Urine Sample Collection

  • Provide a sterile, labeled urine container to the patient.

Patient Instructions

  • Collect midstream urine sample.
  • Label container before sample collection.

Staff Responsibilities

  • Wear gloves when handling urine samples.
  • Perform dipstick testing using standard precautions.
  • Dispose of:
    • Dipsticks → Clinical waste
    • Urine → Sluice/toilet (not sink)

6. Faeces Sample Collection

  • Provide only approved faeces specimen containers.

Labeling Requirements

  • Patient Name
  • Date of Birth
  • Date & Time of Collection

Patient Instructions

  • Wash hands before and after collection.
  • Avoid contamination of container exterior.
  • Seal container securely after collection.

Staff Precautions

  • Always wear gloves.
  • Handle specimens with extreme caution due to infection risk.

7. Microbiological Swabs

  • Ensure swab is placed in transport medium and securely sealed.
  • Do not open the swab container after collection.

Packaging

  • Place swab in biohazard (hazard) bag.
  • Keep requisition form in outer pocket.

If Leakage Occurs

  • Do not handle directly.
  • Dispose of specimen safely as biohazard waste.
  • Arrange for repeat sample collection.
  • Dispose and retake sample

Sample Handling

All samples are handled as per the infection control guidelines

Universal precautions are to be observed while handling samples

Safe Transportation of Samples 

The hospital monitors the transportation of samples from the point of collection to the outsource Lab ensuring the time frame within which the sample has to be processed, and care to be taken to prevent spillage or contamination of the environment or people handling the specimens.

  • The staff nurse on duty to ensure safe transportation of the sample from the ward to the lab for the IPD patient’s samples.
  • All samples requiring transportation are transported in test tubes and further in a well- sealed primary container.
  • All measures are taken so that samples doesn’t deteriorated
  • Necessary precautions are to be taken depending on prevailing environmental factors
  • All outsource sample should be monitor for TAT.
  • During Transpiration Sample will be kept in sample transportation box with required temperature.
  • Sample transportation box will be labelled with biohazard signage’s.

5. SPECIMEN RECEIPT AND PROCESSING AT THE LABORATORY

5.1 Specimen Receipt

  • Upon arrival, the laboratory staff must check and log each specimen.
    • Verify the labeling (patient name, type of test, and collection time).
    • Ensure that the specimens match the accompanying laboratory request forms.
    • Record the time of receipt in the laboratory log.

5.2 Specimen Rejection Criteria

  • Specimens may be rejected if:
    • The labeling is incomplete or incorrect.
    • There is visible leakage or contamination.
    • The container is damaged or improperly sealed.
    • The specimen was transported under improper conditions (e.g., wrong temperature, delayed transport).
  • In case of rejection, notify the healthcare provider immediately and request a repeat sample.

5.3 Specimen Processing

  • Each specimen must be processed according to the specific requirements of the test ordered:
    • Centrifugation: Blood samples may require centrifugation to separate plasma or serum.
    • Culture Setup: Swabs and fluids may require culture media for microbial growth.
    • Histopathology: Tissue samples must be prepared for examination by fixing, embedding, and sectioning.
  • Processing should begin as soon as possible, following the priority level of the specimen.

Disposal of Specimens

All specimen disposal must comply with Biomedical Waste Management (BMW) Rules, 2018.

  • Retention Time

The retention time for paraffin blocks and slides depends on several factors, including specimen viability, storage

capacity, and clinical need. The lower limit for retention is usually 10–20 years.

Destruction

The disposition action for glass specimen slides and paraffin blocks is usually secure destruction or deletion.

Storage

Paraffin blocks and slides should be stored in a humidity-free environment at or below 27°C. Stained slides should

  • be kept away from direct light. Unstained slides should be kept in dry conditions to prevent hydrolysis and preserve
  • proteins.

Retaining slides for digital imaging

If a case has been used to validate digital imaging technology, the slides should be retained.

Retaining slides for molecular diagnostics

Slides can be a "specimen of last resort" when a block has been cut out.

Retaining slides for future testing

  • Unstained slides can be kept for future testing like immunohistochemistry or molecular hybridization

Policy for STAT Samples

  • All STAT samples shall be clearly identified as "STAT/URGENT" on the laboratory requisition form.
  • STAT samples shall receive priority during collection, transport, processing, analysis, validation, and reporting.
  • Delay in STAT reporting beyond the prescribed TAT shall be documented with the reason and reviewed by the Laboratory In-charge.
  • Critical values shall be communicated immediately to the treating clinician and documented in the Critical Value Register. This aligns with your policy on reporting urgent cases and critical results.

Monitoring of Turnaround Time

  • Monthly TAT compliance shall be monitored separately for In-house Routine, STAT, and Outsourced investigations.
  • Delays beyond the defined TAT shall be recorded in the TAT Monitoring Register, investigated, and corrective actions implemented.
  • Outsourced investigations shall also be monitored against the agreed TAT of the referral laboratory, as the policy already requires monitoring of outsourced sample TAT.
